original_value: Neurostimulation has proved to be an effective method for the restoration of visual perception lost due to retinal diseases. However, the clinically available retinal neurostimulation method is based on invasive electrodes, making it a high-cost and high-risk procedure. Recently, ultrasound has been demonstrated to be an effective way to achieve noninvasive neurostimulation. In this work, a novel racing array transducer with a contact lens shape is proposed for ultrasonic retinal stimulation. The transducer is flexible and placed outside the eyeball, similar to the application of a contact lens. Ultrasound emitted from the transducer can reach the retina without passing through the lens, thus greatly minimizing the acoustic absorption in the lens. The discretized Rayleigh–Sommerfeld method was employed for the acoustic field simulation, and patterned stimulation was achieved. A 5 MHz racing array transducer with different element numbers was simulated to optimize the array configuration. The results show that a 512-element racing array is the most appropriate configuration considering the necessary tradeoff between the element number and the stimulation resolution. The stimulation resolution at a focus of 24 mm is about 0.6 mm. The obtained results indicate that the proposed racing array design of the ultrasound transducer can improve the feasibility of an ultrasound retinal prosthesis.

result.paraphrase: Neurostimulation has been shown to effectively restore visual perception lost from retinal diseases. However, clinically available retinal neurostimulation relies on invasive electrodes, which makes it costly and risky. Ultrasound has recently been demonstrated as an effective means of noninvasive neurostimulation. In this study, a new contact-lens-shaped racing array transducer is proposed for ultrasonic retinal stimulation. The flexible transducer is positioned outside the eyeball, like a contact lens. Ultrasound from the transducer reaches the retina without traversing the lens, greatly reducing acoustic absorption in the lens. Acoustic-field simulation used the discretized Rayleigh–Sommerfeld method, and patterned stimulation was achieved. A 5 MHz racing array transducer with varying element counts was simulated to optimize the array configuration. The results indicate that a 512-element racing array is the most suitable configuration when balancing element count and stimulation resolution. At a 24 mm focus, the stimulation resolution is about 0.6 mm. These results suggest that the proposed ultrasound transducer racing array design can enhance the feasibility of an ultrasound retinal prosthesis.
